sources.title: NGSS 4-PS3-4: Apply scientific ideas to design, test, and refine a device that converts energy from one form to another
U.S. Department of Energy: Explore a Wind Turbine (text version)

note.text: The tower lifts the turbine high up, where the wind blows faster. Faster wind means more electricity.

steps.title: Nacelle
steps.instruction: Trace the box at the top of the tower.

note.text: This box, the nacelle, holds the generator: the machine that turns spinning motion into electricity.

steps.title: Blades
steps.instruction: Trace the hub and all three blades.

note.text: Wind pushes on the blades, which are shaped like airplane wings. They spin the hub, which turns a shaft in the nacelle.

steps.title: Wind
steps.instruction: Draw the two arrows of wind blowing in.

note.text: Moving air has energy. The turbine changes the wind's energy of motion into electrical energy.

steps.title: Power line
steps.instruction: Draw the power line from the tower to the house.

note.text: Wires carry the electricity from the turbine to where people use it.

steps.title: House
steps.instruction: Trace the house and its roof.

note.text: In the house, the electricity can change form again: into light from lamps or sound from a radio.

steps.title: Energy's path
steps.why: The wind's motion spins the blades, the generator turns that spinning into electricity, and wires carry it to the house.

steps.title: Improve the design
steps.question: Engineers want this turbine to make more electricity. Which change would help?

options.text: Build a taller tower to reach faster wind
options.feedback: Yes. Wind usually blows faster higher up, and faster wind spins the blades harder, making more electricity.

options.text: Paint the blades a brighter color
options.feedback: Color doesn't change how hard the wind pushes. A taller tower reaches faster wind.
Indoors there's no wind to spin it. It needs to be up in fast-moving air.
The blades catch the wind. A taller tower, reaching faster wind, would help more.
